name: Bahrain
summary: Muslims are governed by Sharia, which guarantees fixed shares; the Constitution (art. 5(d)) makes inheritance a right governed by Islamic Sharia. Non-Muslim foreigners are governed by the law of their own country under Legislative Decree 11 of 1971. Bahrain has a trust law, but the sources found do not settle foundations.
reserved_share: Muslims: fixed Sharia shares (Constitution art. 5(d); Bahrain's family law is largely uncodified and applied case by case by the Sharia courts). Bequests are limited to one third under Sharia (not sourced for Bahrain).
foreign_law_note: Legislative Decree 11 of 1971 on the inheritance and settlement of estates of non-Muslim aliens applies the law of the deceased's country to identify heirs and their shares; with no heirs, the estate goes to the Bahraini Treasury after a year. It applies to non-Muslim foreigners by operation of law, not as a free choice. A Muslim foreigner's estate would follow Sharia.
trust_note: Bahrain has a statutory trust law (reported as Legislative Decree 23 of 2006; number not verified) used for family business planning. Whether Sharia shares can be overridden by a trust over a Muslim's Bahraini assets is untested in the sources found. No private-foundation statute was found (waqf exists for Muslims).
open_questions: Verify the Bahrain trust law's number and scope; the Tamimi article could not be retrieved in full.
No source found on a private foundation law; 'no' is provisional.
Bahraini Supreme Court 2026 decision on foreign Jewish customs in succession (conflictoflaws.net) not read in full.

Hague Trusts Convention: The HCCH status table (checked 2026-10-16) lists 14 Contracting Parties; this country is not one of them and no UK, Dutch or Chinese extension covers it, so the 1985 Convention is not in force here.
